'''Cindy A. Regal''' is an American experimental physicist most noted for her work in [[quantum optics]]; [[atomic, molecular, and optical physics]] (AMO); and [[cavity optomechanics]]. Regal is an associate professor in the Department of Physics at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder|University of Colorado]] and [[JILA]] Fellow;<ref name=JILABio>{{cite web|title=Cindy Regal|url=https://www.colorado.edu/physics/cindy-regal|website=JILA, University of Colorado|access-date=3 March 2019|date=2016-04-04}}</ref> and a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS).<ref name=APSFELLOW>{{cite web|title=APS Fellows, 2016|url=https://www.aps.org/units/damop/fellowship/index.cfm?year=2016|website=American Physical Society|access-date=4 March 2019}}</ref>

==Biography==
Regal was raised in [[Duluth, Minnesota]] and attended [[Lawrence University]].<ref name=duluth>{{cite web|title=Duluth News Tribune|url=https://www.duluthnewstribune.com/lifestyle/2312298-faces|website=Duluth News Tribune|access-date=3 March 2019}}</ref> On a graduate fellowship to CU Boulder from the [[Hertz Foundation]],<ref name=hertz>{{cite web|title=Hertz Fellow Profile|url=https://hertzfoundation.org/fellows/fellow-profile/11139/Cindy-Regal|website=Hertz Foundation|access-date=3 March 2019}}</ref> Regal pioneered experimental techniques for ultracold Fermi gases under the supervision of [[Deborah S. Jin]].<ref name=thesis>{{cite thesis|type=PhD thesis|arxiv = cond-mat/0601054|last1 = Regal|first1 = C.|title = Experimental realization of BCS-BEC crossover physics with a Fermi gas of atoms|last2 = Jin|first2 = D. S.|year = 2006}}</ref> Her PhD thesis, which showed a crossover between [[Bose-Einstein condensation]] and [[superconductivity]] using an [[Ultracold atom|ultracold gas]] of atomic fermions, was awarded the APS Division of AMO Physics (DAMOP) thesis prize in 2007.<ref name=DAMOP>{{cite web|title=APS Honors and Prizes|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?first_nm=Cindy&last_nm=Regal&year=2007|website=American Physical Society|access-date=3 March 2019}}</ref>

After, Regal worked with Dr. Konrad Lehnert at JILA to establish a novel platform for studying the [[nanomechanics]] of a beam capacitively coupled a superconducting transmission-line microwave cavity, which achieved a displacement imprecision of 30 times the [[standard quantum limit]].<ref name=nanobeam>{{cite journal|title=Measuring nanomechanical motion with a microwave cavity interferometer|journal=Nature Physics|volume=4|issue=7|pages=555–560|doi=10.1038/nphys974|year=2008|last1=Regal|first1=C. A.|last2=Teufel|first2=J. D.|last3=Lehnert|first3=K. W.|bibcode=2008arXiv0801.1827R|arxiv=0801.1827|s2cid=118580283}}</ref> Her postdoc in the group of Prof. [[H. Jeff Kimble]] at [[Caltech]] resulted in another novel experimental system for exploring [[cavity optomechanics]], this time using optically levitated [[nanoparticle]]s.<ref name=nanoparticles>{{cite web|title=Caltech Physicists Propose Quantum Entanglement for Motion of Microscopic Objects|url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/caltech-physicists-propose-quantum-entanglement-motion-microscopic-objects-1587|website=Caltech|date=21 December 2009 |access-date=4 March 2019}}</ref> Regal returned to CU Boulder as an assistant professor in physics in January 2010 and became the university's first [[Clare Booth Luce|Clare Booth Luce Professor]].<ref name=CBL>{{cite web|title=Physicist wins CU's first-ever Clare Boothe Luce Professorship Award|url=https://www.colorado.edu/asmagazine/2010/10/01/physicist-wins-cus-first-ever-clare-boothe-luce-professorship-award|website=CU Boulder|access-date=4 March 2019|date=October 2010}}</ref>

The [https://jila.colorado.edu/regal/ Regal Laboratory] studies experimental quantum systems of interacting atoms, photons and phonons. Regal has described this work as seeking “to engineer and explore new quantum systems with controlled connections for quantum information and quantum optics”.<ref name=CBL /> This highly interdisciplinary research <ref name=trampoline>{{cite web|title=Microscopic trampoline may help create networks of quantum computers|url=https://www.colorado.edu/today/2018/07/16/microscopic-trampoline-may-help-create-networks-quantum-computers|website=CU Boulder|access-date=4 March 2019|date=2018-07-16}}</ref> has been recognized by the [[Packard Foundation]] in 2011 <ref name=packard>{{cite web|title=Cindy Regal Wins Packard Fellowship|url=https://www.colorado.edu/physics/2011/10/12/cindy-regal-wins-packard-fellowship|website=CU Boulder|access-date=4 March 2019|date=2011-10-13}}</ref> and the [[Barack Obama]] Administration with a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]] in 2012.<ref name=wh>{{cite web|title=President Obama Honors Outstanding Early Career Scientists|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/07/23/president-obama-honors-outstanding-early-career-scientists|website=Obama White House Archives|access-date=4 March 2019|date=2012-07-23}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
* Fellow, American Physical Society, 2017 <ref name=APSFELLOW />
* Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE), 2012 <ref name=wh />
* Packard Fellowship in Science and Engineering, 2011 <ref name=packard />
* Hertz Foundation doctoral thesis prize winner, 2007 <ref name=hertz />
* APS Division of AMO Physics (DAMOP) thesis prize winner, 2007 <ref name=DAMOP />
* Hertz Foundation Fellowship for graduate studies in the physical sciences, 2001-2006 <ref name=hertz />
